border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">Dad's Advice for How to Live</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">2</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Mar 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Company </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>I was 16 and about to head off as the youngest member of a month-long wilderness sailing trip. The night before my departure my dad came into my room to check on my packing and inspect my gear. He got serious and gave me the following advice for how to stay alive, keep safe and make the most of my time.</p> <p>It has stuck with me. It is the best, most concise advice I know for how to build a startup, be a parent or venture into the unknown.</p> <h3 id="1-show-up"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#1-show-up" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>1. Show up</h3> <p>This is meant in all its forms and in its most expansive definition. Showing up is being physically present, mentally present and emotionally present. It means showing up with an attitude of engagement.</p> <h3 id="2-pay-attention"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#2-pay-attention" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>2. Pay attention</h3> <p>So often our minds and our bodies live in two different places. Being present and paying attention to both the internal and external is shockingly hard. The people around us can tell when we are checked in or checked out mentally or emotionally. As a parent I've learned that kids are shockingly good at detecting emotional attention (or distraction ;).</p> <h3 id="3-do-what-needs-to-be-done"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#3-do-what-needs-to-be-done" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>3. Do what needs to be done</h3> <p>This could mean carrying bags, cooking dinner, starting to sing to keep spirits up, offering help or asking for help. It is about identifying the need and doing it (or helping) regardless of "shoulds" or "jobs". Sometimes what needs to be done is letting someone struggle through a task they are learning. Being with them sometimes is what needs to be done. </p> <h3 id="4-dont-agree-if-you-dont-agree"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#4-dont-agree-if-you-dont-agree" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>4. Don’t agree if you don’t agree</h3> <p>In the context of the wilderness this meant if I wasn’t comfortable with the risks I needed to speak up. Sometimes keeping the group together is more important than the route that is taken. In those cases agree to keep the group together and disagree on the route. I've heard others describe this as "disagree then commit." This means taking a duty to fully express my opinion when we are discussing our plans. Then fully committing to making whichever plan we pick a success.</p> <h3 id="5-be-open-to-outcome"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#5-be-open-to-outcome" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>5. Be open to outcome</h3> <p>This is the most philosophical. This is also the hardest for me. It is about not wasting energy on: worrying, fretting, anguish or anger. Still care passionately about what I am doing, that I should have strong preferences. Work hard to create those outcomes I desire. But let go of the belief that I am the only force in the world. This is about focusing on the process used to make a decision, and not the result.</p> <p>Thanks dad ❤️</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">Why I Started Cyclic</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jun 2021 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> general </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>At my last company we had a micro-services architecture. We also focused on recruiting developers who were smart and dedicated, but not yet experienced. When they started we would task them to add some new functionality. This would require on the order of perhaps 20 to 50 lines of business logic.</p> <p>However this would require 500 to 1000 lines of infrastructure code. Between project setup, framework config and infrastructure as code yaml, the actual purpose of the service was drowned out. The gearing ratio was all wrong.</p> <p>When these developers went to build and deploy, they would encounter more troubles. If you have ever worked with AWS you will know that CloudFormation is not known for the predictability or clarity of its errors. If you have worked with API Gateway and Lambda you will know how quickly you can get lost in a dark thicket of abstractions and frameworks, each blurring and bending into the the next.</p> <p>Even when the infrastructure would provision without error the call paths and observability was lacking. The infinite power combined with the lack of knowledge of where to start reminded me of staring at the blinking command prompt the first time I loaded linux. "Something is happening in here, I just don't know how or where"</p> <p>I believe as experienced engineers we too often default to expecting those coming behind us to spend their time learning the same lessons we learned. Instead I want to clear the way for not yet experienced developers to go beyond what I have been able to accomplish. To do this we need new tools. And we need a new abstraction.</p> <p>Our vision is a world where you write your hello world on your local and then publish it in a way the whole world can use it immediately. No where in that process do you size servers or design fail-over health checks. Instead you just worry about what you want to say.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>‍</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">The VC Business Model and Why VCs Invest</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">8</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jun 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Company </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>(photo credit <a href="https://wonderstorms.substack.com/p/how-can-we-fix-the-market-for-solutions" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Charles Cushing</a>)</p> <p>This article is intended for startup founders, particularly for those who are first timers. There is nothing extraordinary about my VC experiences. I have done the following: raised an angel round and two institutional rounds (and failed at two rounds?) at a company I co-founded in the GovTech/Community space (SeeClickFix). I have participated in pitches as CTO of a pre-PMF (product market fit) mortgage tech company (HeavyWater). I have raised a friends-and-family round at my current Cloud Infrastructure company (<a href="https://www.cyclic.sh" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://www.cyclic.sh</a>)</p> <p>‍</p> <p>The venture funding landscape is evolving. It seems there is more innovation now than at any other time. My goal here is to explain the general case so that you have a reference point for understanding the more novel or innovative approaches. Aka there are exceptions to everything here, but first let us learn the base case.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>The majority of the confusion or difficulty I had raising Venture Capital was that I didn’t fully understand the VC business model. I didn’t understand the individual investors and their incentives. I didn’t appreciate the incentives for the fund itself. Nor did I understand what the fund’s investors (Limited Partners aka LPs) were expecting. Hopefully this will help you understand what I didn’t.</p> <p>‍</p> <h1 id="the-vc-business-model"><a href="#the-vc-business-model" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>The VC business model</h1> <p>‍</p> <p>Venture funds are companies. Their purpose for existence is to make money from making investments in other companies.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>They are composed of Limited Partners (LPs) and a General Partner (GP). The GP is the company owned and run by the "VC" you meet at some networking event. The VC has formed these companies and raised money from LPs. Part of the structure of the fund is that it will exist for no more than 10 years. At the end of that time all proceeds or investment holdings will be sent back to the LPs (minus any fees for the GP).</p> <p>‍</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/625dce5fe5890977b45753cb_vc-structure-angellist.png"></p> <p>VC Fund Structure (photo credit <a href="https://learn.angellist.com/articles/venture-capital-fund#toc_8_H2" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Angel List</a>)</p> <p>‍</p> <p>‍</p> <p>The LPs invest in the fund because they want to make money. The "Limited" in LP refers to the time the investor doesn’t spend working in the business. They send a check and that is their involvement.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>The VC formed the GP and raised money from the LPs because they want to make money. The GP charges a management fee of 2% per year on assets the LP invests with the fund.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>The GP will charge carry, aka 20% of any profits from the investments they make. The LPs get to first recover their initial investment, including those 2% fees, then any additional profits are shared with the GP.</p> <p>‍</p> <h1 id="the-lifecycle-of-a-single-vc-fund"><a href="#the-lifecycle-of-a-single-vc-fund" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>The Lifecycle of a single VC fund</h1> <p>‍</p> <p>Just as VC funds have standard structures and standard fees, they have a standard development and lifecycle. Understanding where a particular fund is in this progression will help you understand their expected behavior. Also, a single VC might have multiple funds that are in different stages of this trajectory. I have found that VCs are very open and willing to talk about which fund they are actively investing out of, how big it is, when they raised it and their average check size. I have always been able to find this information by asking.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="first-years-load-up-the-plate"><a href="#first-years-load-up-the-plate" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>First Years: Load up the Plate</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>As a new entrepreneur I didn't realize how critical time fit with a VC was. After they raise from their investors (LPs) they are on a time crunch to get the money invested. They want to invest in good companies but they only have about 1-3 years to invest. This means it is much easier to raise from a VC who has just raised. They are rapidly putting money to work. They just arrived at the buffet with an empty plate. Everything looks good and they don't have anything that is a better alternative already on their plate.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="middle-years-getting-picky"><a href="#middle-years-getting-picky" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Middle Years: Getting Picky</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>After that first phase they transition into a slower but still active investment role. In this 4-6 year middle window a VC will still take meetings but are much less likely to make new investments. At this phase they have a full plate but are still wandering around the buffet looking for great options. The threshold is now higher for inclusion. They may prefer the truffle parm fries they just found (your company), but they already have cajun curly fries which are almost as good (a company they already invested in). However they may have raised a new fund so they could be in two phases at once - make sure to ask!</p> <p>‍</p> <p>These VCs won't tell you that they probably won't invest. They are happy to ask questions and probe into your business. They get tremendous market intelligence from taking these meetings. They get to see:</p> <ul> <li> <p>What people are pitching (deal flow)</p> </li> <li> <p>How is the market is responding to these pitches?</p> </li> <li> <p>Do you raise quickly? Do you struggle to raise? At what price? On what terms?</p> </li> <li> <p>Benchmark strategy data for their current portfolio companies eg Are social ads working? What is your customer acquisition cost? What are your churn rates?</p> </li> <li> <p>Potential insights for their current portfolio companies</p> </li> <li> <p>Optionality of investing in an amazing company/founder eg maybe your company is the best investment they have seen in their professional life</p> </li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="final-years-the-tail-end-finishing-up"><a href="#final-years-the-tail-end-finishing-up" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Final Years the Tail End: Finishing up</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>At this point they have transitioned to harvesting or running off the portfolio. They are returning funds to investors. They know that their investment fund will close after 7-10 years so this is a period of actively winding down.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>At the buffet they have switched to dessert and coffee. It would be an extraordinary turn of events such that you could convince them to take a scoop of some new main course. More likely they have raised another fund, probably at the end of the first year or two and any pitch would get investment from that fund. So effectively that VC is "loading their plate" even if one of their funds is in this phase of winding down.</p> <p>‍</p> <h1 id="outcome-fit"><a href="#outcome-fit" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Outcome Fit</h1> <p>‍</p> <p>A natural tendency when considering an endeavor (business or other) is to start with the likelihood of success. This line of thinking asks how probable each outcome is. It is a frame of thinking that trades size of outcome for certainty in outcome. Increasing certainty can raise the floor on returns, but also lower the ceiling.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>When the VC was raising money from LPs they put together a spreadsheet that described the basic economics of the venture fund. Roughly it modeled the following for 10 investments:</p> <ul> <li> <p>5 will fail completely, the investments will be a complete loss</p> </li> <li> <p>3 will do ok, they will each return somewhere between 3x</p> </li> <li> <p>1 will do great, it will return 10x</p> </li> <li> <p>1 will do amazing, it will return 25x+</p> </li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <p>This would put the fund in the top-1% of VCs. A more likely outcome of those 10 investments is:</p> <ul> <li>6 will fail</li> <li>3 will do ok they will each return on average ~3x</li> <li>1 will do great, it will return ~5x</li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <p>This would put the VC roughly at the median returns for all VC firms. You can read more over at this <a href="https://www.toptal.com/finance/venture-capital-consultants/venture-capital-portfolio-strategy#strike-outs-dont-matter-in-vc" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">great break down of VC returns</a>.</p> <p>‍</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/625dd037e0bac549cf18edf9_venture-returns-sethlevine.png"></p> <p>Distribution of Returns on VC Investments (credit: <a href="https://www.sethlevine.com/archives/2014/08/venture-outcomes-are-even-more-skewed-than-you-think.html" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Seth Levine</a>)</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Let us step back and look at your company from the VC's perspective for a moment. They are evaluating if your company has the potential of returning 10-50x the investment they make. Only if the company passes that screen will they engage on if your company has a reasonable risk adjusted chance of making that outcome a reality.</p> <p>‍</p> <h1 id="conclusion"><a href="#conclusion" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Conclusion</h1> <p>‍</p> <p>The tech twitter joke of "big if true" can be a helpful tldr guide for how VCs evaluate potential investments. Make sure you know where they are in their investing lifecycle to ensure you are spending your time wisely. Hopefully this was helpful. If you have any questions or if I wasn’t completely clear find me on twitter: <a href="https://twitter.com/seekayel" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">@seekayel</a></p> <p>‍</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. src="/_nuxt/image/9c3ff8.webp" width="1280" height="800" alt="Considerations for Serverless Active-Active: Routing" sizes="(max-width: 640px) 340px, (max-width: 768px) 400px, (max-width: 1024px) 600px, 1200px" srcset="/_nuxt/image/3ed23e.webp 340w, /_nuxt/image/e8a4f3.webp 400w, /_nuxt/image/a52732.webp 600w, /_nuxt/image/9c3ff8.webp 1200w" class="w-full rounded-2xl"> <div class="space-y-8 border-b border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">Considerations for Serverless Active-Active: Routing</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">8</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jun 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Mike Korostelev</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> AWS </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p><em>(Part 1 of a series)</em></p> <p>Building active-active in multiple regions can be expensive and complex. Serverless-native applications can make it simpler to serve users globally and enable more effective recoveries with less effort.</p> <p>Starting from the end user making an http request and assuming there are two identical instances of an application running in two AWS regions - this and next several posts will discuss considerations, tools and solutions for building serverless active-active architectures.</p> <h2 id="routing"><a href="#routing" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Routing</strong></h2> <p>The first touchpoint for a request is DNS routing. This where the cloud DNS (<a href="https://aws.amazon.com/route53/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">AWS Route53</a>) connects the request to your application's endpoints - in whatever region they are in the world.</p> <h4 id="which-regional-instance-of-the-application-to-send-the-request-to"><a href="#which-regional-instance-of-the-application-to-send-the-request-to" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Which regional instance of the application to send the request to?</h4> <p>AWS Route53 lets you select a routing policy for DNS records. A regional policy will route users the closest geographic region ($0.70 per million queries). A latency policy will route to the the lowest query latency record ($0.60 per million queries). For high traffic web services, the TTL value should be considered as most web clients cache dns for the specified TTL.</p> <p>If the record is configured as an alias to an AWS service (like cloudfront and api gateway) - the dns queries are free.</p> <h4 id="how-to-know-that-the-instance-in-the-region-is-actually-healthy--before-routing-the-request"><a href="#how-to-know-that-the-instance-in-the-region-is-actually-healthy--before-routing-the-request" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to know that the instance in the region is actually healthy ✅ before routing the request?</h4> <p>If a region is down (and it's not even your fault), Route53 does not know not to send requests there. To make Route53 know the state of an endpoint, health checks can be configured. Depending on the config, a health check is somewhere between $0.50 - $2.00 per month. Two ways to configure a health check are:</p> <ul> <li>Monitor an endpoint by continuously polling it from multiple regions - this will result in multiple requests per second to some endpoint where your application responds with some kind of 200. Since all these requests must be handled by something and can get expensive downstream from the traffic generated by the health check itself.</li> <li>Monitor cloudwatch alarms - this lets you be more creative about what ‘healthy’ means and can go both ways on cost/complexity. This option is likely going to have more lag than monitoring an endpoint directly.</li> </ul> <p>Here the TTL is a more important consideration - since clients will cache dns - faster health-check polling intervals will not give you instantaneous routing switchover. So if users are actively using a service at the moment the switch over happens, you should have the expectation that they may still be hitting the failing endpoint until their dns cache expires.</p> <p><strong><em>The next few posts will discuss these and other considerations, approaches and dirty hacks for building a low overhead active-active strategy with serverless on AWS:</em></strong></p> <h4 id="compute"><a href="#compute" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Compute</strong></h4> <h5 id="how-to-process-the-requests-in-both-regions-without-having-to-pay-for-two-computes"><a href="#how-to-process-the-requests-in-both-regions-without-having-to-pay-for-two-computes" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to process the requests in both regions without having to pay for two computes?</h5> <h5 id="how-to-scale-capacity-if-suddenly-a-single-regional-application-instance-must-pick-up-the-slack-for-a-whole-other-regions-worth-of-traffic"><a href="#how-to-scale-capacity-if-suddenly-a-single-regional-application-instance-must-pick-up-the-slack-for-a-whole-other-regions-worth-of-traffic" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to scale capacity if suddenly a single regional application instance must pick up the slack for a whole other region’s worth of traffic?</h5> <h4 id="data"><a href="#data" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Data</strong></h4> <h5 id="how-to-make-sure-the-data-created-by-either-regional-application-instance-is-available-to-the-other"><a href="#how-to-make-sure-the-data-created-by-either-regional-application-instance-is-available-to-the-other" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to make sure the data created by either regional application instance is available to the other?</h5> <h4 id="ops"><a href="#ops" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Ops</strong></h4> <h5 id="human-decisions-are-political-decisions-politics-takes-time-in-a-disaster-time-is-scarce---how-to-remove-humans-from-the-process"><a href="#human-decisions-are-political-decisions-politics-takes-time-in-a-disaster-time-is-scarce---how-to-remove-humans-from-the-process" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Human decisions are political decisions, politics takes time, in a disaster time is scarce - how to remove humans from the process?</h5> <h5 id="how-to-manage-infrastructure-across-multiple-regions-without-multiplying-operational-overhead"><a href="#how-to-manage-infrastructure-across-multiple-regions-without-multiplying-operational-overhead" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to manage infrastructure across multiple regions without multiplying operational overhead?</h5> <h4 id="latency"><a href="#latency" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Latency</strong></h4> <h5 id="how-to-deal-with-eventual-consistency-and-the-fact-that-data-replication-is-not-instantaneous"><a href="#how-to-deal-with-eventual-consistency-and-the-fact-that-data-replication-is-not-instantaneous" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to deal with eventual consistency and the fact that data replication is not instantaneous?</h5> <p>‍</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 border-b border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">Write Shitty Code - why you should and feel good about it</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Feb 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Engineering </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>I know how to write good code.</p> <p>Usually it means spending more time now to make the code better for some future state of the world. This assumes that I know what the future will look like. In software we rarely know what the future holds.</p> <blockquote> <p>In software we rarely know what the future holds</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <p>Uncertainty can be caused by:</p> <ul> <li>Not knowing the technology</li> <li>Not knowing the business</li> <li>Not knowing the user</li> <li>Not knowing the data size of the system</li> <li>Not knowing the longevity of the code</li> <li>Unknown-unknowns (see 2020 for more complete list of examples)</li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <p>When I have uncertainty about the future, cycle time is most important. It allows me to capture value from my code by: learning as quickly as possible, minimizing impacts of bad or faulty code, as well as shortening my time to market.</p> <p>Any friction hurts my cycle time. This decreases the rate I can turn uncertainty into certainty aka learning. My longest term value is created by learning as quickly as possible, since it is a multiplier for all future code I write or systems I design. Said another way: As "writing is re-writing" coding is refactoring.</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>My longest term value is created by learning as quickly as possible</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <p>Here is why you should write shitty code. Or more precisely, why you should write MORE shitty code.</p> <p>‍</p> <h3 id="build-the-skill-of-writing-code"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#build-the-skill-of-writing-code" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Build the skill of writing code</h3> <p>If you want to learn how to write code the best way to develop that skill is practice. I have found I can read all I want, but I don’t retain the lesson until I type the code with my fingers. Coding is a skill that is not learned in a day. It is a way of thinking and approaching problems. It is a collection of knowledge about tools and computing environments. The only way to develop this knowledge is to use the tools and environments. Each time I write code the easier and less shitty the next time will be.</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>Each time I write code the easier and less shitty the next time will be</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <h3 id="reconnect-with-the-joy-of-creation"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#reconnect-with-the-joy-of-creation" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Reconnect with the joy of creation</h3> <p>Writing shitty code means focusing on getting to the outcome as quickly as possible. This means getting to that feeling of success and satisfaction that something, anything is working. I wrote my first line of code about three decades ago, I still get a thrill each time I get a new piece of code working.</p> <p>‍</p> <h3 id="learn-how-code-and-systems-fail"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#learn-how-code-and-systems-fail" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Learn how code and systems fail</h3> <p>Systems fail. I have found that these are the most precious opportunities to learn. My biggest learnings have come not from making some quality trade-off I anticipated, it was some behavior or input to the system that I never even considered. If I spend time building something that is “flawless” I am emotionally invested in it working. Then, when something goes wrong I look for errors external to the code I wrote.</p> <p>When I write shitty code I have no emotional attachment to it functioning. When it fails I assume it is the weakest link and dive into learning more about the code and system. This mental state is a state of wonder and joy.</p> <p>No code runs wholly in isolation. Each unexpected failure (by definition) is something that I didn’t understand. Therefore each failure is a perfectly crafted lesson that is adaptively constructed for me to maximize my learning.</p> <h3 id="learn-how-to-debug"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#learn-how-to-debug" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Learn how to debug</h3> <p>When I code I have several standard loops of feedback. When I write shitty code I turn up the frequency of those feedback loops. This naturally puts pressure on me to understand where to look and how to look for output from the code I am writing. Each time I write code I learn more about my tools. I could learn a new keyboard short-cut for my editor or I could write a script for some manual step in the testing process. The point is that each time I write code I improve the quality of my tools and my understanding of those tools.</p> <h3 id="explore-the-design-space"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#explore-the-design-space" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Explore the design space</h3> <p>If I am writing code to do something that I am unfamiliar with, which is basically all the code I write, because otherwise it would be refactoring, I don’t know the design space. I don’t know what is possible because I don’t know what I don’t know.</p> <p>In drawing classes sometimes they assign variation studies. Basically you come up with 5 or 10 initial sketches from some prompt. Then you draw 5 or 10 variations of each. This is an exploration of the design space. Sometimes I find myself comparing two possible designs. This is a limitation on what is truly possible. There are more likely to be dozens of different possible designs. Writing more shitty code lets me see more of what is possible. I look up from where I stand and see the whole landscape of possibility.</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>Writing more shitty code lets me see more of what is possible</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <p>‍</p> <h3 id="lowered-expectations-releases-more-creative-energy-and-thoughts"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#lowered-expectations-releases-more-creative-energy-and-thoughts" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Lowered expectations releases more creative energy and thoughts</h3> <p>I know I mentioned this in previous reasons, however the change in emotional state I experience when I let go of the ego of my code being “right”, is monumental. Instead of feeling frustration or irritation I feel wonder, discovery, joy and a sense of accomplishment. Even if all the other reasons are wrong, the difference in personal emotional state is worth writing more shitty code.</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>Instead of feeling frustration or irritation I feel wonder, discovery, joy</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <h3 id="conclusion"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#conclusion" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Conclusion:</h3> <p>A lot of senior experienced people will talk about all the “shoulds” your code should be like. They are usually describing some far distance promised land that they have never visited either. Some of these “shoulds” are packaged as frameworks to help think through tradeoffs in system design. The best have an explicit out clause for knowing when the rules don’t apply. In the end they are helpful if they guide you, and are not if they slow you down.</p> <p>Said another way, know where you are headed but embrace the shittyness of producing code for today.</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">Users Are the Best Feature</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Feb 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Product </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>As an engineer I like to talk about the features of a product. I talk about the product’s implementation and how it was built. I get excited about the internal workings. I have spent days of my life working on features that were never used. I operated under a mental framework that users came from outside and were external to the product. I was concerned with building the product. The users would be there when I was done. So I spent most of my time heads down writing code.</p> <blockquote> <p>So I spent most of my time heads down writing code.</p> </blockquote> <p>During college I spent a whole summer internship building an automated test case generation program for network router configurations. While building that product I only did one session with the engineers I expected to use the product. It was a presentation late in the summer. I wrote no documentation.</p> <p>The program was never used after I went back to school. I am sure this is a tale that is familiar to many in the software community. Spend months of time to build something that once completed is immediately scrapped.</p> <blockquote> <p>The program was never used after I went back to school.</p> </blockquote> <p>It is a cautionary tale of building without user feedback and not building usage along with building the product. At the time I told myself: the company had problems; it was their fault they couldn't see the value in the tooling I built.</p> <p>Now, I have come to realize: users are a feature. They are the best feature. With users a product is alive and useful. If I want users then I need to spend time working on that feature.</p> <blockquote> <p>Users are a feature. They are the best feature. With users a product is alive and useful.</p> </blockquote> <p>There are several ways to work on the users feature. Whether I spend time acquiring, educating, activating, retaining, supporting, scaling or nurturing them, I need to do it with the same intentionality and focus as I work on any other feature. Again, users are a feature. And, they are the best, most important, and hardest feature there is.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>So you agree? Great!</p> <p>‍</p> <h4 id="what-is-next"><a href="#what-is-next" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>What is next?</h4> <p>How do we magically "get" users? Where is the "hello world" for user acquisition? Where is the "npm init" for this feature?</p> <p>Well this post series is an attempt to catalogue the specific tactics and actions that have worked for me.</p> <p>‍</p> <h4 id="posts-in-this-series"><a href="#posts-in-this-series" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Posts in this series:</h4> <ul> <li>Users: Going from 0 to 1 (coming soon)</li> <li>Users: Going from 1 to 10 (coming soon)</li> <li>Users: Going from 10 to 100 (coming soon)</li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <h4 id="resources"><a href="#resources" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Resources</h4> <p>Other people have great write ups on what might work in general, current favorites:</p> <ul> <li><a href="https://www.goodreads.com/pt/book/show/24693635-traction" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Traction: How Any Startup Can Achieve Explosive Customer Growth</a> (book on channels)</li> <li><a href="https://www.first1000.co/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">First 1000</a> (substack of case studies)</li> <li>Which others?</li> </ul> <p>‍</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div class="space-y-8 border-b border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">How to go from 0 to 1 - Growing users for a new product or service</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Feb 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Product </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>As a repeat founder I get the question from entrepreneurs and others: "how do you get your first users?"</p> <p>For me, this is actually the easiest stage. I think of acquiring and growing a group of users differently based on the scale of the existing user base. There is a great book that talks about going 0 to 1 (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero%5C_to%5C_One" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero\_to\_One</a>). What I mean here is how to go from 0 users to 1 user.</p> <p>In this case the first user is ... You.</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>Use your product before you launch.</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <p>You are the first user. Use your product before you launch. Every day. Selling meal kits? Well you eat every day don't you? There are very few startups where you can't be trying the product prior to launch on a daily or weekly basis.</p> <p>The absolute best would be to go through the full onboarding process as a new user. Sometimes that is impractical. Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good here. Daily is better than weekly, weekly is better than monthly. Set yourself a recurring meeting for an hour weekly.</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good</p> </blockquote> <p>Right after college I worked for an online bank. I insisted that I be an account holder. And I used the account. This didn’t immediately make me exactly like the other users of the site, but it gave me a grasp of the feel of the product.</p> <p>When I was a cofounder of a citizen engagement service, I didn't use the platform daily and I think it showed. I wasn't immersed in the experience of being a user. I was external, guessing what users might want.</p> <p>Now at Cyclic I try to push code everyday. The best days are when I build a new starter example and try to deploy for the first time. If you </p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>I try to push code everyday</p> </blockquote> <p>Using my own products, I find I'm annoyed by the incomplete features. Small ux issues can really grate on me. I think this is the point.</p> <p>Repeat after me: "I am the first user. I am user number 1"</p> <p>‍</p> <blockquote> <p>I am the first user. I am user number 1</p> </blockquote></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">AWS Tools Suck</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Feb 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> AWS </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>If you have ever worked with AWS as a developer then you will know what I mean, AWS tools suck. They suck so bad there is an entire industry focused on solving for this pile of suck. For just Infrastructure as Code, for example, there are Terraform, Pulumi and Serverless. AWS is famous for "listening to customers". So what gives? Why do their tools still feel clunky, complex and riddled with infuriating edge cases?</p> <h3 id="tldr"><a href="#tldr" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>tldr</h3> <p>You, the developer, are not the customer.</p> <p>The longer answer is a combination of several factors. Here are my three reasons for why things are the way they are.</p> <h3 id="reason-1-aws-never-was-a-developer-tools-company"><a href="#reason-1-aws-never-was-a-developer-tools-company" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Reason 1: AWS never was a developer tools company</h3> <p>AWS never won based on having the best experience or tooling. They offered one powerful value proposition, you could shorten your project lead time by using their services. You no longer need to do capacity planning for the number of disks (s3), servers (ec2) or network capacity (egregious egress). Oh, and they were fanatical about availability.</p> <h3 id="reason-2-aws-doesnt-sell-based-on-dev-ex"><a href="#reason-2-aws-doesnt-sell-based-on-dev-ex" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Reason 2: AWS doesn't sell based on Dev Ex</h3> <p>AWS is growing at least as faster than the cloud market as a whole [1], yet they have below average developer experience. The only way that this can happen is if their customers are purchasing for reasons other than quality of developer tools. If the decision maker cared about developer experience why do they keep choosing AWS? The only reasonable answer is the person picking doesn't prioritize Dev Experience over some other attributes of the vendor (that is for another post).</p> <h3 id="reason-3-if-aws-wanted-it-they-would-have-it"><a href="#reason-3-if-aws-wanted-it-they-would-have-it" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Reason 3: If AWS wanted it they would have it</h3> <p>Given the near 1 billion dollar a week capital expense annual run rate AWS was at in Q4 of 2020 [2], if it was of strategic importance for them to solve for better tooling they would. This is not a case of "not enough resources'', this is a case of the project not getting the internal priority to invest in improvement.</p> <h3 id="conclusion"><a href="#conclusion" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Conclusion</h3> <p>AWS continues to grow despite having bad tooling and developer experience. If it impacted their sales they would make it a priority. If they made it a priority to have great tooling, they would have it. The only conclusion is: bad tooling isn't affecting their sales. Therefore, sales decisions aren't being made at the level or for the reasons that developer tooling changes the outcome.</p> <p>Which means AWS tools will continue to suck for the foreseeable future.</p> <p>[1] <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2021/08/02/cloud-infrastructure-market-kept-growing-in-q2-reaching-42b/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://techcrunch.com/2021/08/02/cloud-infrastructure-market-kept-growing-in-q2-reaching-42b/</a></p> <p>[2] <a href="https://www.platformonomics.com/2021/03/follow-the-capex-oracle-fy21-q3-update/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://www.platformonomics.com/2021/03/follow-the-capex-oracle-fy21-q3-update/</a></p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">AWS Budget Alerts Based on Cost</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Feb 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> general </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>If you have used AWS you know how costs can sneak up on you. I have experience getting a heart stopping bill at a previous startup. With Cyclic I've decided I want to start adding controls and alerts from the start.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>I recently found that AWS added Cloud Formation support for Budgets (<a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-budgets-budget.html" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">AWS::Budgets::Budget</a>). You can create a quick budget to to notify you of either actual COST limits or FORECASTED cost limits. Here is a sample Cloud Formation example.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>I have also been working on setting up <a href="https://spike.sh" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">spike.sh</a> to use for an incident management and alerting platform. They accept SNS webhooks. So two Cloud Formation stacks later we can now get the budgets.amazonaws.com principal to publish alerts to an SNS topic that fires an https webhook at our spike.sh integration URL. This will trigger an incident and alerts.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Launch a budget into your account:</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Of course it wouldn't be AWS without a few sharp edges. So here are the caveats:</p> <ul> <li>We are publishing the "Launch Stack" button templates on Github. However Cloud Formation only accepts s3 urls for template bodies</li> <li>We are creating the S3 bucket to host the templates with Cloud Formation. However despite Requestor Pays being 7 years old there is no Cloud Formation support. Funny how Cfn requires S3 but then makes it hard to use Cfn to setup hosting of the templates (<a href="https://github.com/aws-cloudformation/cloudformation-coverage-roadmap/issues/123" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">github issue</a>)</li> <li>SNS topic policies only allows named service principals eg: 'budgets.amazonaws.com' for some reason '*' is invalid.</li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <p>All code can be found in this github repository (<a href="https://github.com/cyclic-software/budget-sns-alerts" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">cyclic-software/budget-sns-alerts</a>)</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Let us know what you think and if you find this helpful.</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">AngelList Roll Up Vehicles: Why, What and How</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Feb 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Company </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>I recently raised a friends and family round for Cyclic and used an AngelList Roll Up Vehicle (RUV). More on the round later. Multiple founder friends have asked about my experience and why I used an RUV. Here is the Why, What and How:</p> <h1 id="tldr"><a href="#tldr" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>TL;DR</strong></h1> <blockquote> <p>A Roll Up Vehicle is a legal entity that can take investments from multiple investors or entities and then invest that money as a single entity on your company’s cap table. Here are the pros and cons for using an AngelList RUV as part of a venture capital fundraising round:</p> </blockquote> <p>‍</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/61034dd64ba727b1f9120503_angellist_ruv.png"></p> <p>Visual depiction of how investments are rolled up onto your captable</p> <h2 id="pros"><a href="#pros" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Pros</strong>:</h2> <ul> <li>Future rounds are simplified, exactly when most stressful</li> <li>Future rounds are cheaper ($)</li> <li>Investor's address and info is kept private</li> <li>Simplified e-signature and funding for investors and company at time of investment</li> </ul> <h3></h3> <h2 id="cons"><a href="#cons" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Cons</strong>:</h2> <ul> <li> <p>Some additional setup for the company (~1hr)</p> </li> <li> <p>Small additional cost (now only filing fees <a href="https://www.angellist.com/blog/eliminating-fees-for-roll-up-vehicles" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://www.angellist.com/blog/eliminating-fees-for-roll-up-vehicles</a>)</p> </li> <li> <p>Additional complexity describing to your investor who AngelList is and how they are involved</p> </li> </ul> <h3 id="should-i-use-a-ruv"><a href="#should-i-use-a-ruv" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Should I use a RUV?</strong></h3> <p>I would definitely recommend an AngelList RUV to anyone raising an early venture capital round where:</p> <ul> <li> <p>You expect to raise another round in the future </p> </li> </ul> <p>And one or more of these to apply:</p> <ul> <li> <p>You have 10 or more angels</p> </li> <li> <p>You have angels that do less than 4 deals a year</p> </li> <li> <p>You have angels writing checks for less than $25k</p> </li> </ul> <h3 id="cyclic---what-we-do"><a href="#cyclic---what-we-do" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Cyclic - What we do</strong></h3> <p>As a developer the complexity to go from your local to the cloud is increasing. This is driving cloud platform selection into a pre-design time decision. We are dedicated to solving both of these problems for developers. Our goal is to let you push to deploy while making cloud environment selection a runtime decision. Sign up for the <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Cyclic Private Beta</a><br> ‍ <a href="https://deploy.cyclic.sh/cyclic-software/starter-express-api" target="_blank"> <img format="webp" loading="lazy" src="https://deploy.cyclic.sh/button.svg"> </a></p> <h3 id="my-past-experience"><a href="#my-past-experience" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>My Past Experience</strong></h3> <p>At the last company I co-founded, we raised a convertible note and then two priced rounds over the course of 7 years. The deal terms were reasonably standard for VC deals. They included drag along provisions. We were first time founders and I think we did an "ok" job of keeping all of our investors updated on how the company was doing.</p> <p>Despite drag along rights (i.e. company able to "drag" small investors into a transaction if some percentage of shares in the company agree to the transaction), the lawyers involved with our second priced round wanted signed docs from all investors along with consent of spouse docs for any investment held by a person instead of trust or other entity. This meant that we needed to coordinate outreach to roughly ten angel investors, most of whom were non-professional angels. We needed to bring them up to speed on why we were raising, and explain we needed their signatures on documents for the round even though the company had drag along rights. Oh and by the way, we needed signatures from their spouses as well, leading them to have the same conversation with less fidelity with their spouse.</p> <p>The more experienced angels who had larger checks generally understood the process and were more likely to have entities which they used to make the original investment. So they were either less likely to have questions and most were able to be a sole signer on behalf of the entity that held the investment. The converse of this was also true. The smaller check angels were more likely to have questions, they were less familiar with what was standard and they were more likely to need signatures from a spouse. Additionally, it seemed that the less experienced angels were less engaged with email and had longer turn around times.</p> <p>In a vacuum, handling each of these conversations is manageable. However, once a closing date was set, all of these small "punch list" items seemed to bubble to the surface. It seemed that there was a spike in the length of items remaining once the date was set. The 7 to 14 days before closing are among the most stressful for a co-founder. In my experience, having extra tasks and communication on my plate was extra stress at exactly the wrong time.</p> <blockquote> <p>The 7 to 14 days before closing are among the most stressful for a co-founder... having extra tasks and communication on my plate was extra stress at exactly the wrong time.</p> </blockquote> <h3 id="why-an-ruv"><a href="#why-an-ruv" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Why an RUV</strong></h3> <p>The RUV prevents the need to keep going back to the early angels. It is a legal structure where the angels have already agreed that someone designed by the RUV organizer will be able to sign future docs related to their investment. The designated person can sign any future fundraising documents. In my case, I am that designated signer.</p> <p>This means at the next funding round I will be able to sign on behalf of the RUV. So for a bit more time and cost upfront (and maybe a bit more complex conversation with the angels) I am able to decrease my complexity (and stress) at the time of each future funding round.</p> <h3 id="how-it-works-for-founders"><a href="#how-it-works-for-founders" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>How it works for Founders</strong></h3> <p>Sign up and on-boarding were easy. I wrote a blurb on the company, uploaded a deck or memo, filled in some deal terms, identified notable co/lead-investors, targeted raise amount, and selected how I would pay the RUV fee (either company pays or investors pay). I didn’t have the exact form of the SAFE complete when I set up the RUV, it is only required at close, provided it is substantially the same terms as any of the listed co/lead investors.</p> <p>For me there was some email back and forth with the AngelList team since they were still doing a staged rollout when I signed up. I had some questions during setup and emailed with two people who work at AngelList. Both were responsive and helpful. The email support felt personal and attentive.</p> <p>My only complaints on the company product side are that the UI/UX was a bit complicated for just doing the RUV. It seemed it was more focused on syndicates and funds. If there is any "product" work for the AngelList team this is probably where it is. For example: to get to the RUV page you navigate via the "Deals" menu item and the deal is listed under my "Syndicate". This all sorta makes sense given the product is essentially a Syndicate where the fee and carry are 0%. However it doesn’t really make sense when I am the company founder doing a RUV. Additionally I didn’t find a way to set a per investor minimum, perhaps I just missed it in interface. These are minor points of friction but they left me with a feeling that it was still an early product that wasn’t fully polished yet.</p> <h3 id="how-it-works-for-investors"><a href="#how-it-works-for-investors" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>How it works for Investors</strong></h3> <p>The investor side was smooth even for first time angels investing either personally or through an entity. The flow has e-signature to the RUV docs and the ability to enter bank account details so AngelList can initiate an ACH (electronic transfer). There is also the ability for the investors to wire if that is their preference.</p> <p>That is literally it. Smooth and easy.</p> <h3 id="thoughts-questions"><a href="#thoughts-questions" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Thoughts? Questions?</h3> <p>‍</p> <p>Let me know what you think. Did you find this helpful? Do you still have questions?</p> <p>‍</p> <p>You can: <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Signup for Cyclic</a></p> <p>‍</p> <p>Shoot me an email: <a href="mailto:kam.lasater@cyclic.sh">kam.lasater@cyclic.sh</a></p> <p>‍</p> <p>Give me a shout out on twitter: <a href="https://twitter.com/seekayel" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://twitter.com/seekayel</a></p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div
