nuxt-content"><h2 id="everyone-fails-at-software-they-dont-build"><a href="#everyone-fails-at-software-they-dont-build" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Everyone fails at software they don't build</h2> <p>There are three types of software systems that any company runs. First, high value software systems that drive customer value. Second, the systems necessary to deliver the product or service, but not sufficient as stand alone products on their own. Third, systems that support the business but are not related to the competitive advantage of the company. The fourth type of software system is one that doesn’t exist. Every company has software they chose not to build. This is "Unbuilt Software". To understand how much value organizations are missing out on, we must first better understand each type of software system and how software investment decisions are made.</p> <h4 id="tier-1---high-value-systems"><a href="#tier-1---high-value-systems" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Tier 1 - High Value Systems</h4> <p>These systems or services compose the key building blocks for the company. They are the services that set the standard for what other software in the company will comply with. Meaning their requirements for security, performance, or quality set the standards other software at the organization is expected to meet. Since they are the highest value, they dictate what language and frameworks will be used and what architectural and hosting patterns are used by engineers in the company. These systems establish the culture and establish what skills are high status inside of the engineering groups.</p> <h4 id="tier-2---necessary-systems"><a href="#tier-2---necessary-systems" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Tier 2 - Necessary Systems</h4> <p>The second type of software systems are software systems that are necessary but not sufficient for the company to exist. These are systems that will use the frameworks, languages, testing processes, release methodology, and security frameworks that the high value systems use. These systems are important for the company but do not drive the same outsized value of Tier 1 systems, hence they do not warrant the same level of investment to create new policies, procedures, or technologies.</p> <h4 id="tier-3---supporting-systems"><a href="#tier-3---supporting-systems" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Tier 3 - Supporting Systems</h4> <p>Companies have other systems that are necessary for the company to exist. If the company was to be formed again they might not even be internal to the company, but at this point it would cost more to migrate to some other provider than to just stay. This is the classic: "We have been running X for years. It works fine. Why do we need to spend money to switch?" These systems are usually one-off ancillary systems handled by a particular department that has a rollup of functionality underneath them; this is often the domain of an IT operations group.</p> <hr> <h4 id="how-to-fail---tier-1"><a href="#how-to-fail---tier-1" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to fail - Tier 1</h4> <p>You can fail at the first type of system by not truly understanding the constraints in which you are operating. These systems might have very high levels of requirement for performance. For example, If the engineers do not understand the mechanisms and are not schooled in the particular technologies or optimization required to meet those objectives, this can become an existential threat to the company.</p> <h4 id="how-to-fail---tier-2"><a href="#how-to-fail---tier-2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to fail - Tier 2</h4> <p>You can cause the second type of system to fail by overly constraining their ability to be improved. If the security and build processes needed in the first type of systems constrain the second type of system such that they do not and are not upgraded and improved, they will fall out of pace with the industry. This creates an opportunity for competitors to enter the market with improved efficiencies around the second types of systems, which lowers their overall cost basis. Unfortunately, this can then become an existential threat to the company.</p> <h4 id="how-to-fail---tier-3"><a href="#how-to-fail---tier-3" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to fail - Tier 3</h4> <p>A way to fail with the third type of system is to not understand the sunk cost fallacy. These systems are necessary, but any additional investment is throwing good money after bad. If they are so critical that they are necessary for the business to operate then they must be considered one of the other types of systems. It seems the primary way to fail with these types of systems is to let them absorb budget and time from the business beyond their business value.</p> <p>It’s much better to take three days or a week of downtime at your convenience and at known time versus to risk having the system fail completely when you are unprepared and possibly a critical time for your business. Any effort or any investment of time and money should be focused on migrating or eliminating the systems all together. It is much better to have an account with a company whose business it is to provide that service as that company's first priority versus to have it as an afterthought or red-headed stepchild within yours.</p> <h4 id="how-to-fail---tier-4-the-software-you-dont-build"><a href="#how-to-fail---tier-4-the-software-you-dont-build" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to fail - Tier 4 The software you don’t build</h4> <p>What this analysis leaves out is the types of systems that do not exist. These are the systems that are speculative. When building software, oftentimes, the full value of the system does not become apparent till the system is beyond a prototype. Invention and innovation are created through experimentation. If the constraints of an organization's build and deployment systems limit the range of software that an individual may build, then the organization will limit the value of the software they may build because they are not able to anticipate the value created by the experiments.</p> <p>Any minimum fixed cost of building software will cause the organization only to build projects that have reasonable certainty of exceeding the cost of building them. Organizations struggle to prioritize building software that is hard to quantify the value of a system. Examples are tools that more quickly surface information from multiple sources for employees, tools that eliminate communication between groups, or tools that reduce delay for individuals.</p> <p>If the value of software systems is distributed as a power law then to increase value you should take more samples from the distribution. This implies that it is most important to increase the number of potential opportunities to have a runaway success. If the only way to experiment is to pay the tax of complying with Tier 1 processes, you’re sentencing your organization to a decreased amount of innovation.</p> <hr> <h3 id="a-way-out"><a href="#a-way-out" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>A way out</h3> <p>One way to increase the number of experiments is to enable the largest number of individuals in your organization to conceive of and implement these experiments. Each organization has some individuals who are able to do so without assistance. A system that enables them to do so with less friction and less difficulty will increase the frequency that they experiment. Lowering the difficulty will also increase the number of individuals in your organization that are able to experiment. This means creating a way for individuals to rapidly prototype new ideas outside of the usual constraints of Tier 1 systems, but in a way that they can evolve into Tier 1 systems. This capability is a strategic advantage to an organization. Having an experimentation system will create long term value for the organization.</p> <p><strong>Has your software team found a way to succeed at Tier 4? Visit us in our <a href="https://discord.cyclic.sh" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Discord community</a> and share your successes.</strong></p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. src="/_nuxt/image/94ffbb.webp" width="1280" height="800" alt="How to Debug" sizes="(max-width: 640px) 340px, (max-width: 768px) 400px, (max-width: 1024px) 600px, 1200px" srcset="/_nuxt/image/0eaa2f.webp 340w, /_nuxt/image/49eb08.webp 400w, /_nuxt/image/08b102.webp 600w, /_nuxt/image/94ffbb.webp 1200w" class="w-full rounded-2xl"> <div class="space-y-8 border-b border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">How to Debug</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">13</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jun 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Engineering </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>We all hit bugs that feel impossible to diagnose. The hardest ones to debug are intermittent or inconsistent. How do I fix what works sometimes? If a line of code always breaks then the fix is direct. The system is linear. The action leads to a failure.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>How do I debug a bug that is intermittent? How do I debug something that works sometimes?</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Here are some reminders to myself next time I encounter a baffling debugging session.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="choose-learning"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#choose-learning" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Choose Learning</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>My greatest learnings come from debugging. This bug is an opportunity for me to learn more about this system. If I already knew what was causing the problem then I wouldn't have a bug. The fact that I have a bug that isn’t obvious to me on how to fix, by definition means I have a chance to learn.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>The system is giving me the gift of the chance to learn.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Choose to take the opportunity to learn.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="chase-the-error"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#chase-the-error" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Chase the Error</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>Answer the question: "how do I make this fail every single time?"</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Instead of continuing to make the system work. Instead make the system fail. Go straight at the error. Maximize it. Increase the error rate. Trigger the error repeatedly.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Focus on driving the error rate to 100%. Only then can I be sure any success is from my action and not inconsistency.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Make predictions to test my understanding: "The system will fail, now (pushes button)"</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="simplify"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#simplify" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Simplify</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>Once I can create the error on demand, I isolate. I begin simplifying the steps to trigger. Remove steps or hard code responses. Trim excess complexity not needed to cause error.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>If it takes 6 steps to reproduce, try turning each one off in order.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Find the minimum degrees of freedom to still reproduce the error.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="assess-the-inverse"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#assess-the-inverse" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Assess the Inverse</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>Reminder: the error is not caused by something I understand. Look explicitly for areas where I assume the system is working.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>What are the parts of the system that I am sure are working? What if they weren’t working as I expected? Verify the components are actually working as I expect.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Reminder: It’s not what we don’t know that gets us into trouble, it is what we know for sure that isn't true</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="devise-a-conclusive-measure"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#devise-a-conclusive-measure" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Devise a Conclusive Measure</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>Brainstorm what report, measure, logging or data would definitely tell me what is causing the error. Maybe this won't tell me "why" the error is happening, but point me closer to "where" the error is being caused.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Question: What piece of information would conclusively tell me what the problem was?</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="take-a-break"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#take-a-break" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Take a Break</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>I might be making things worse. If I don’t know what causes the error I don’t know if I’m making it worse. If the situation allows for it, take a break.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Get some air. Go for a walk. Breath.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>A clear relaxed mind is open for new ideas.</p> <p>‍</p> <p>Sleep on it. Pick it up tomorrow.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="explain-how-to-reproduce"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#explain-how-to-reproduce" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Explain How to Reproduce</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>Say it out loud.</p> <p>Talk to myself.</p> <p>Explain the steps to reproduce.</p> <p>Start at the beginning.</p> <p>Back up three steps and explain again.</p> <p>Slower this time.</p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="summary"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#summary" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Summary</h2> <p>‍</p> <p>Hopefully this helps you debug an issue you are struggling with. If you have other techniques or improvements to these let me know: twitter.com/seekayel</p> <p>‍</p> <p>For those who jump to the end, here is the tldr:</p> <p>‍</p> <ol> <li>Choose Learning</li> <li>Chase the Error</li> <li>Simplify</li> <li>Assess the Inverse</li> <li>Devise a Conclusive Measure</li> <li>Take a Break</li> <li>Explain How to Reproduce</li> </ol> <p>‍</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">6 Command line Tools All Experts Know</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">13</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jun 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Engineering </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>I work on Mac OSX and Linux command line environments. My tool kit is shaped by the needs I have. This is my tool box of tools that work with almost any command and help me go from just using the command line to being an expert.</p> <p>Wow, your friends and colleagues. These tools make every other command at the command line more powerful.</p> <h2 id="-aka-pipe"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#-aka-pipe" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>| (aka pipe)</strong></h2> <p>Pipe is awesome. It lets me connect the output of one command and "pipe" it into the input of another command. This is the universal glue that instantly lets me level up the effectiveness of my command line usage.</p> <h3 id="gotchas"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#gotchas" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Gotchas</strong></h3> <p>There are two outputs from each command, standard out (stdout) and standard error (stderr). Pipe by default connects to stdout.</p> <h2 id="--aka-dash"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#--aka-dash" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>- (aka dash)</strong></h2> <p>Some commands take a file name as an argument. In cases where I want to use stdin or stdout. Dash is the answer.</p> <p>I use this alot when I want to read a file from s3 and display it to the console or take the output from a command and write the file to s3.</p> <p>Print file to console: <code>aws s3 cp s3://some-bucket-name/awesome-file.json -</code></p> <h2 id="pbpaste-and-pbcopy"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#pbpaste-and-pbcopy" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong><code>pbpaste</code> and <code>pbcopy</code></strong></h2> <p>These are technically commands as well. They interact with the paste buffer.</p> <p>On mac you can access your paste buffer using the paste-buffer-paste (pbpaste) and paste-buffer-copy (pbcopy) commands. I love how they keep my console clean especially when I have trying to transform a large chunk of text/json</p> <p>Example:</p> <p><code>aws s3 cp s3://some-bucket-name/awesome-file.json - | pbcopy</code></p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="xargs"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#xargs" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>xargs</strong></h2> <p>This is technically a command. It is a command that executes commands.</p> <p>It executes a command for every line of input it receives. The arguments you pass to xargs form the basis of the command to execute.</p> <p>Hint: use <code>-J{}</code> to substitute <code>{}</code> (or some other character string) in the middle of the command to execute or multiple times for that matter.</p> <p>Example: <code>pbpaste | xargs -J{} aws s3 cp {} -</code></p> <p>‍</p> <h2 id="2-and-21"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#2-and-21" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong><code>2></code> and <code>2>&1</code></strong></h2> <p>Sometimes I want to send stderr somewhere else other than the console. Using its number is the way.</p> <p>Send to trash: <code>2>/dev/null</code></p> <p>Send to error log: <code>2> error-log.txt</code></p> <p>Combine with stdout: <code>2>&1</code></p> <h2 id="ctl-z--fg"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#ctl-z--fg" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Ctl-z + fg</strong></h2> <p>Suspend the foreground process, run some other commands, then return the suspended process to the foreground.</p> <h2 id="man----n"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#man----n" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>man + / + n</strong></h2> <p>When I know the command but not the exact syntax my first source of information is the manual. Instead of searching google I search the manual.</p> <p>Example: <code>man xargs</code> then <code>/utility</code> advance to next found instance with <code>n</code></p> <p>‍</p> <p>‍</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">How to Fail at Serverless: Serverless is Stateless</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">11</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jul 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> AWS </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>This blog series is an extended version of a talk I gave at <a href="https://nyc.serverlessdays.io/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Serverless Days NYC 2022</a>. The goal is to share ways that a "friend of mine" has failed at serverless to help level up the community. Just as the transportation industry shares accident report analysis with the whole industry to improve safety, we in the software community need to do the same. This is my attempt to do that.</p> <p>I'm sure there is some product X that has feature Y that fixes issue Z. I either didn't know about it at the time, didn't have the budget, couldn't get it through vendor/security review, product wouldn’t schedule it with our engineers or it didn't comply with enterprise architecture's plan for our software roadmap. As some guy once said: "You go to production with the tools you have, not the tools you want."</p> <p><strong>Note:</strong> ‍</p> <ul> <li>Names have been changed to protect the innocent and not so innocent.</li> <li>Only egos (and wallets) were harmed by the failures recounted here.</li> </ul> <h2 id="serverless-is-stateless"><a href="#serverless-is-stateless" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Serverless is Stateless</h2> <p>All the architecture posts talk about serverless as stateless computing. How serverless is so scalable because it scales out to satisfy increased load, and scales in when not needed. This all makes sense. Lambda is like a big thread pool in the sky. Got it.</p> <p>I can set some parameters to manage the maximum and minimum number of threads and AWS would handle all the hard work of hosting, spinning up, spinning down and networking the instances together. Awesome-sauce.</p> <p>‍</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/62c86713fed3b513be122ce8_i-dont-remember.gif"></p> <p>lambda be like</p> <p>Well, almost...</p> <h3 id="use-case"><a href="#use-case" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Use Case</h3> <p>Background job that receives batches (10's-100's) of PDFs from the client, splits them apart into individual pages (1-1000 per PDF) and does analysis on each page. The arrival rate from the client is lumpy. Primarily US working hours on a 5 min interval. Response is measured in hours. This feels like a perfect HelloWorld use case for StepFunctions doing orchestration and Lambda doing image manipulation.</p> <h4 id="lambda-logic"><a href="#lambda-logic" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Lambda logic:</h4> <ul> <li>Invoke with S3 path to file</li> <li>Read 10+mb files from S3 to /tmp</li> <li>Process file</li> <li>Write results to S3</li> <li>Respond with S3 path to transformed file</li> </ul> <p>‍</p> <p>Serverless FTW!</p> <p>Everything works great until... inconsistent out of disk space errors, or no space left on device (depending on your OS/language stack).</p> <h2 id="how-to-fail"><a href="#how-to-fail" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to Fail</h2> <h3 id="problem"><a href="#problem" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Problem</h3> <p>Periodically a step function run will fail due to a Lambda invoke failing on no space left on device (or similar depending on os and language). Running the same file in dev/test doesn't reproduce the error. Re-running the step function in production succeeds.</p> <p>‍</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/62c866a26c2399e457733a1f_lambda-pac-man.png"></p> <p>lambda pac man loves eating data and leaving it in /tmp</p> <h3 id="solution"><a href="#solution" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Solution</strong></h3> <p>Well... lambda instances have a writable <code>/tmp</code> folder where you can store temporary files. And somewhere in the AWS docs they describe how instances of your Lambda function are reused between invocations.</p> <p>Some quick googling gets you a solution of clearing <code>/tmp</code> at the start and/or end of each invocation (<a href="https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44108712/aws-lambda-release-tmp-storage-after-each-execution" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">stack overflow ftw</a>). Till that fix makes it to production you can just re-execute any failed step function runs.</p> <p>Nothing quite like shipping code copy-pasted from Stack Overflow. Nice.</p> <p>Success! Party!</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/62c867cdc310db14bbac6405_leo-congrats.gif"></p> <p>Stack Overflow code FTW!</p> <p>‍</p> <p>until... wait what? out of memory errors? WTF!</p> <h3 id="problem-v2"><a href="#problem-v2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a><strong>Problem v2</strong></h3> <p>Periodically a step function run fails. The Lambda invoke error is no memory left (or similar depending on os and language). Running the same file in dev/test doesn't reproduce the error. Re-running the step function in production succeeds. Turning on debug or releasing new builds adding additional logging suppress the error rate. WTF (why the failure?) Load tests don't reproduce the error.</p> <p>The explanation that AWS just fails on 1 in ~100k lambda invokes starts to wear thin with your Ops team that is getting paged to click a button. But we could just automate the re-run!</p> <p>Deep inside accepting it "just fails" violates some axiom about how computers works. This is knowable and damn-it I shall know. So you strap the lambda down setting max concurrency to 1. Turn up the load test. Let’s do this.</p> <p>At 12k documents the lambda invoke fails for out of memory. Interesting.</p> <p>Rerun the load test. At 12k documents the lambda invoke fails for out of memory.</p> <p>If an error is repeatable it isn't random. 12k is an important number. It also happens to be the maximum number of file descriptors allowed for the linux OS the lambda is running on.</p> <p>Back to google. Apparently the image manipulation library I am using has a history of bugs with leaving open file descriptors. Looks like each invoke to lambda is leaving another file descriptor open in the OS file descriptor table.</p> <p>The lambda will then fail when it hits 12k unless it is recycled. The lambda instance can be recycled due to:</p> <ul> <li> <p>a code deployment: new code, new instances</p> </li> <li> <p>update to environment variable: hence why turning on debugging suppressed errors.</p> </li> <li> <p>scaling down: a burst in load will scale out new instances and then scale back down. Only some instances survive.</p> </li> </ul> <h3 id="solution-v2"><a href="#solution-v2" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Solution v2</h3> <p>Expand the IAM role permissions to allow the lambda permission to update itself (your security team might give you side eye for this, fair warning, send them this blog post, I'm sure it will convince them).</p> <p>After completing the work of an invoke, call the lambda api to set an environment variable to a random value. We dubbed this the "self-immolation" solution.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/62c868256c23997e757361fa_lambda-self-immolation.png"></p> <p>This lambda will self destruct in 3... 2... 1...</p> <p>Hacky? Yeah.</p> <p>Chaos for the lambda team? Probably.</p> <h3 id="yolo-"><a href="#yolo-" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>YOLO 🤷</h3> <p>Did it work? Yes.</p> <p>Stay tuned, for more stories of #fail.</p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">You Too Can Deploy Static Sites on Cylic</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">23</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jan 2023 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Rachel Schipull</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> engineering </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><h2 id="did-you-know-you-have-options"><a href="#did-you-know-you-have-options" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Did you know you have options?</h2> <p>Most builds on Cyclic are as easy as hitting that bright green “Deploy” button and waiting for your confetti. However some take a little more setup.</p> <p>It’s still easy, it’s still fun, it just takes a little more “know how.”</p> <p>So let’s look at one of our most powerful tools to get things done and maximize your deploying power on Cyclic: Build Options.</p> <p>Over my next couple posts, I’m going to go through some of the most popular ways to use Build Options and we’ll have a little fun.</p> <h4 id="but-first-where-do-you-find-them"><a href="#but-first-where-do-you-find-them" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>But first, where do you find them?</h4> <p>There are two places to find Build Options in Cyclic, which really have to do with when you’ll need them.</p> <ol> <li>You can access build options from the “Advanced” dropdown right before you connect a repo: <img alt="" src="/content/build_options_1.png"></li> <li>You can find the Build Options in the “Environments” tab after your build is complete: <img alt="" src="/content/build_options_2.png"></li> </ol> <p>Alright, now you know where to find them, so what do you do with them? Let's start with one simple way to use Build Options. In this post, we’re going to start nice and easy and deploy a static site.</p> <h2 id="static-sites"><a href="#static-sites" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Static Sites</h2> <p>If you aren’t familiar with the term “static site,” you may think of them as client-side only websites. A classic example would be a resume site or a portfolio site. In this case you only need to serve a frontend. There’s no database, no GET, no POST, no CRUD. You get the picture.</p> <p>However, because of how Cyclic reads your repo to make sure it’s ready to go, currently you’ll still need to add a package.json file for Cyclic to deploy it. That means we still need Node.js baybeeee!</p> <p>I'm going to run through this process with a fun little project I made a while back... a calculator called Sneaky Calc. It's just html, vanilla css, and a little JavaScript that makes the calculator calculate. Classic static site.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/calculator.png"></p> <p>Now, that we have chosen a project to host, let's get our Node on.</p> <p>If we have Node installed already, this is a piece of cake. If not, I recommend heading to the Node.js website and starting with Node’s recommendation for how to install it on your operating system <a href="https://nodejs.org/en/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://nodejs.org/</a>.</p> <p>Once Node.js is on board, we can move on to the next step.</p> <p>If our frontend website (html, css, and maybe some client-side javascript) is working properly in the local environment, we'll go ahead and run <code>npm init</code> in the root directory of the project (in the terminal).</p> <p>Node will run us through a brief setup of our package.json file. In most cases, we just have to hit enter until the file is added to our project root folder. You can always customize your package.json, but for a static site, it doesn’t really matter.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/packageJSONSetup.png"></p> <p>The final piece of setup is to add the start script <code>”start”: node index.js</code> to scripts in our brand new package.json file. Cyclic specifically looks for the node start script to give us access to the screen with the ✨Advanced Build Options✨.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/addNodeScript.png"></p> <p>Yes, we know, we don’t specifically have an “index.js” file in this application. It’s ok. Just go with it.</p> <p>Now we're going to push our brand new package.json file up to Github and get ready to deploy on Cyclic.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/ReadyToDeploy.png"></p> <p>As soon as we get to the Connect screen we are going to hit “Advanced” and toggle “Static site” to the “on” position.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/ReadyToDeployAdvanced.png"> <img alt="" src="/content/ToggleON.png"></p> <p>We'll hit the Connect button now and BINGO! That calculatin' static site is 🎉live🎉 and hosted on Cyclic.</p> <p>And just to hammer it home, if we head over to the dashboard, we can see the Static Site toggle is turned on there as well, nice: <img alt="" src="/content/afterDeployToggle.png"></p> <p>So there it is, the simplest use for Advanced Build Options and the first step on our journey towards understanding how to use all the bells and whistles Cyclic has to offer.</p> <p>Prefer a video overview of this process? Check it out below: <a href="https://youtu.be/-B98D6x8mBg" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"><img alt="" src="/content/youtubestatic.jpg"></a></p> <p>I'll have more on Build Options soon, but if you have questions in the meantime, come chat with us in Discord: <a href="https://discord.cyclic.sh" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">discord.cyclic.sh</a>.</p> <p><em>Want to see the cheat codes on my Sneaky Calc, <a href="https://sneakycalc.cyclic.app" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">click here</a>.</em></p></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">Cyclinks: Build a Linktree Clone on Cyclic</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">10</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Mar 2023 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Rachel Schipull</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Engineering </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><h2 id="cyclinks-for-everyone"><a href="#cyclinks-for-everyone" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Cyclinks for everyone!</h2> <p>Why use a pre-built link sharing service and share your data when you can build your own? In this tutorial, we'll use Create React App, TailwindCSS, and Cyclic.sh to help you set up your very own link site.</p> <p><strong>Wanna fast forward and just use the template?</strong> Check out the <a href="https://github.com/cyclic-software/cyclinks" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Cyclinks repo here</a>.</p> <hr> <p>First things first, let's kick it off by creating a new React app with Create React App. You can do that in a fresh repo locally by following the Create React App <a href="https://create-react-app.dev/docs/getting-started/" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">documentation</a> but we've made it even easier by setting up a starter in <a href="https://cyclic.sh" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Cyclic.sh</a> which you can fork from our Start Template tab.</p> <p>If you want, you can fork the starter right here: <a href="https://deploy.cyclic.sh/cyclic-software/starter-react-app"> <img format="webp" src="https://deploy.cyclic.sh/button.svg" alt="Deploy on Cyclic" loading="lazy"> </a></p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/createreact.png"></p> <p>Once you have forked and cloned this repo locally, take a second to <code>npm install</code> to install the included dependencies that come with the starter.</p> <p>The next step is to install TailwindCSS. Don't be intimidated by Tailwind, it just takes a couple steps to get it working.</p> <p>First, <code>npm install -D tailwindcss</code> and then run the command <code>npx tailwind init</code> to create a 'tailwind.config.js' file.</p> <p>In the Tailwind config file, you need to give it access to the content you would like Tailwind to be able to affect. Under content add <code>'./src/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}',</code> and <code>'./src/components/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}'</code></p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/exports.png"></p> <p>There's so much more you can add to the Tailwind config file, but for now we'll head over to 'App.css' and add the following bottom of the file:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>@tailwind base; @tailwind components; @tailwind utilities; </code></pre></div> <p>This adds the Tailwind to your CSS so that all the layers are able to access Tailwind's capabilities. Nice! Let's move on to the application.</p> <p>First things first, if you want to see what Create React App looks like fresh out the gate, use the command <code>npm run dev</code>. That should spin up a version of the template on "<a href="https://localhost:3000" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://localhost:3000</a>" and you can check it out.</p> <p>If you run the application right, now we'll see a standard template from Create React App. There are a few things built in that we can keep, other things we'll modify, the rest can be ignored or trashed.</p> <p>The public folder holds a lot of the information that indicates what the website is to the world, such as the favicon, index.html containing the “root”, and a manifest with metadata.</p> <p>I swapped the React favicon for a Cyclic Favicon and updated the manifest.json to reflect what I'd like the site to be called: CycLinks… obviously. And so it immediately reflects the change in the browser tab.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/updatedtab.png"></p> <p>Cool, so how do we get these sick links set up?</p> <p>Well currently, everything that is being rendered is entered directly into the App.js file. We need to make some components that will be imported into that file and those components will compose our links page. Alright? Sweet.</p> <p>Inside the src folder, add a components folder. Inside the component folder, add a file for the following:</p> <ul> <li>Header.js</li> <li>Cyclinks.js (you can call it Links.js if you want)</li> <li>Footer.js</li> </ul> <p>First, we'll go to the 'Header.js' file. If you want your headshot or a profile pic in the header, you'll want to add that to the 'src' folder. Once you've done that you can import it at the top of the file like so:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>import profilepicrs from '../profilepicrs.jpg' </code></pre></div> <p>We'll then create the Header function that will be exported. You can use the styling I've provided with TailwindCSS below. Just a few notes:</p> <ul> <li>In React, remember to use <code>className</code> instead of <code>class</code>.</li> <li>The <code>img</code> tag will style the image.</li> <li>The <code>h1</code> tag is for your name or alias, I have it set up to be animated and pulse between two colors of blue, but that's easily changed to a different color or made static.</li> <li>The <code>p</code> tag is for your title or tagline.</li> <li>For more information on how to style items in TailwindCSS be sure to check out their style guide.</li> </ul> <p>Get your Header component going on:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>function Header() { return ( <header className="container flex text-center mx-auto py-10"> <div className="md:w-4/6 mx-auto"> <img format="webp" loading="lazy" src={profilepicrs} className="h-24 rounded-full mx-auto mb-5 border-white border-double" /> <h1 className="text-xl font-bold text-blue-400 dark:text-blue-200 font-semibold animate-pulse">My Name</h1> <p className='text-white'>My Cool Tagline</p> </div> </header> ); }
export default Header; </code></pre></div> <p>The next part is the meat of the project, it's where we get our LINKS!!</p> <p>First, you need to add a file called <code>cyclinks.json</code> (you could also just call it <code>links.json</code>, but what's the fun in that?). You'll need to create your json with the following format:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>[ { “title": "My link”, "url": "https://link.com" "emoji": "😎" } ] </code></pre></div> <p>You can add as many links as you want, just remember to add a comma between the blocks. If you want to leave the emoji out, just leave the quotes blank.</p> <p>Great! Once you have your link data added in, save the json file and let's set up the Cyclinks.js component.</p> <p>If you've worked with React before, you know you'll need to import the json file:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>import links from '../Cyclinks.json' </code></pre></div> <p>Then like in the Header.js, we'll need to create our component function.</p> <p>The basic functionality of this code is that we're mapping through the list of links in your Cyclinks.json and adding Tailwind styling to them so they arrange themselves in a nice unordered list on our page.</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>function LinkList() { return ( <main className="flex px-3 sm:px-0"> <ul className="w-full md:w-4/5 lg:w-3/6 mx-auto"> {links.map(link => ( <li className="mb-4" key={link.title}> <a className="relative transition duration-200 font-bold bg-blue-400 border-blue-400 border-2 hover:bg-transparent py-4 w-100 block text-center text-white hover:text-blue-400 rounded-lg pl-12 md:px-12" href={link.url} alt={link.title} target="_blank" rel="noopener" > <span className="text-3xl absolute left-0 top-0 bottom-0 pl-3 flex items-center">{link.emoji}</span> <span>{link.title}</span> </a> </li> ))} </ul> </main> ) }
export default LinkList;
</code></pre></div> <p>Finally, we'll create a Footer component. It's not even necessary, but it looks nice to have something at the bottom. This is where we've indicated that we used React to make this project with the CycLinks repo, but you can change it to a copyright or a quote of your choosing.</p> <blockquote> <p>Pro tip, if you want to get free credit on Cyclic, you could even drop a “Deployed on Cyclic” link here and use your referral link. Every little bit counts, right?</p> </blockquote> <p>Anyways, the footer doesn't need to import anything, it's just a component function, styled with Tailwind. The only special effect I used here was the same animation I used to make my name glow.</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>function Footer() { return ( <footer className="px-3 sm:px-0"> <div className="container text-center mx-auto"> <div className="md:w-4/6 mx-auto"> <p className='py-4 text-center text-xs sm:text-sm font-light text-white'> Created with{' '} <span className='text-green-600 dark:text-green-400 font-semibold animate-pulse'> <a href="https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app">React</a> </span>{' '} from{' '} <span className='text-blue-500 dark:text-blue-300 font-semibold animate-pulse'> <a href="https://github.com/rachelschipull/cyclinks">CycLinks</a> </span> </p> </div> </div> </footer> ); }
export default Footer; </code></pre></div> <hr> <p>Nice so let's add these components to the App.js and see what it looks like so far!</p> <p>In App.js, you'll need to make sure import the following:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>import Header from './components/Header' import Cyclinks from './components/Cyclinks' import Footer from './components/Footer' </code></pre></div> <p>Then within the App function, you'll need to replace the Create React App template with our three components inside the top level <code><div></code>.</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code>function App() { return ( <div className="App"> <Header /> <Cyclinks /> <Footer /> </div> ); } </code></pre></div> <p>Don't take out the <code>export default App;</code> at the bottom! That's important.</p> <p>Ok, let's see how it looks.</p> <p>Enter <code>npm run dev</code> in the terminal and you should see something to the effect of:</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/compiled.png"></p> <p>Head to '<a href="https://localhost:3000" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://localhost:3000</a>' and take a look.</p> <p>If your project did not compile successfully, you will get pretty descriptive error messages. Take a look at the file and line number to see if you misspelled a variable or forgot to update something from my code to yours.</p> <p>So this is our app, but we can make it better.</p> <p>I decided to add a background image of stars (because why not). That update went in the 'App.css', as would any other specific changes to a part of the CSS that are outside of Tailwind.</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code> text-align: center; background-image: url(./background2.jpg); } </code></pre></div> <p>Because it was added to the App, I needed to adjust the style in the App.js as well so that the image wasn't cut off in different viewports. I accomplished this by adding a style tag to the <code><div></code> encompassing all the components.</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="language-text line-numbers"><code><div className="App" style={{height:'100vh'}}> </code></pre></div> <p>Ahhh, the finished project:</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/cyclinksss.png"></p> <p>There are a few optimizations I'd like to create for this project. For example:</p> <ul> <li>A parallax effect for the background image.</li> <li>Dropdown previews for the links</li> <li>A shimmering hover effect</li> <li>A variety of link colors</li> <li>Using Font Awesome icons instead of or in additiona to emoji</li> </ul> <p>What ideas do you have for making Cyclinks cooler? Let me know or submit a PR: <a href="https://github.com/cyclic-software/cyclinks" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://github.com/cyclic-software/cyclinks</a>. Have ideas for other demos or tutorials you want to see, drop us a line in <a href="https://discord.cyclic.sh" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Discord</a>.</p> <p>Get started with Cyclinks right now:</p> <a href="https://deploy.cyclic.sh/cyclic-software/cyclinks"> <img format="webp" loading="lazy" src="https://deploy.cyclic.sh/button.svg"> </a></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><h1 id="files-with-secrets-in-nodejs"><a href="#files-with-secrets-in-nodejs" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Files with Secrets in Nodejs</h1> <p>In our journey as Node.js developers, we often deal with various external services such as Google Cloud or Firebase. These services require us to provide credentials that authenticate our application and grant it the necessary permissions to interact with the respective service. This post is about to handle large secrets or files that contain private keys. Google provides files like this. You will see them named a few different things: <code>serviceAccount.json</code> or sometimes <code>serviceAccountCredentials.json</code>. This file contains secret data and is used to authenticate against Google Cloud and/or Firebase.</p> <h2 id="why-an-account-service-json-file-is-needed-for-google-andor-firebase"><a href="#why-an-account-service-json-file-is-needed-for-google-andor-firebase" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Why an Account Service JSON File is Needed for Google and/or Firebase</h2> <p>Google and Firebase provide us with a JSON files that contains private keys for our application to access their services. These JSON files, often referred to as "account service" files, contain the necessary credentials our application needs to authenticate itself with Google and Firebase.</p> <p>The JSON file includes several important pieces of information such as the <code>project_id</code>, <code>private_key</code>, and <code>client_email</code>. This data is crucial for establishing an authenticated communication channel between our application and the respective service. Without this JSON file, our application won't be able to authenticate itself, thus not being able to access or interact with the resources provided by Google Cloud or Firebase.</p> <h2 id="why-the-serviceaccountjson-file-needs-to-be-kept-secret"><a href="#why-the-serviceaccountjson-file-needs-to-be-kept-secret" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Why the serviceAccount.json File Needs to be Kept Secret</h2> <p>As you can guess from the information contained within the JSON file, it's crucial that we keep these files secret and safe. If this file falls into the wrong hands, malicious users could use our <code>private_key</code> to impersonate our application and misuse the services, causing serious security issues. They could potentially access our Firebase data, use our Google Cloud resources, and even incur costs on our Google Cloud account.</p> <h2 id="problems-with-storing-the-file-as-a-string-in-environment-variables"><a href="#problems-with-storing-the-file-as-a-string-in-environment-variables" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Problems with Storing the File as a String in Environment Variables</h2> <p>A common practice is to store sensitive data in environment variables. If you do this on AWS Lambda you can run into an issue. AWS Lambda limits the total size of all <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-envvars.html#:~:text=The%20total%20size%20of%20all%20environment%20variables%20doesn%27t%20exceed%204%20KB." rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">environment variables to a maximum of 4KB</a>. Our JSON file along with a few other variables can easily exceed this limit, making it impossible to store the entire file in an environment variable. Worse case scenario is you are able to deploy your code and you only hit the environment variable size limit when you try to update another variable on some future release.</p> <h2 id="why-you-shouldnt-commit-secrets-to-your-git-repo"><a href="#why-you-shouldnt-commit-secrets-to-your-git-repo" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Why You Shouldn't Commit Secrets to Your Git Repo</h2> <p>It might seem convenient to just commit the JSON file to our Git repository, but yeah, that is a very bad idea. Once a file is committed to a Git repository, its history remains there even if the file is later removed. This means that anyone with access to our repository can find and use these secrets.</p> <p>If our repository is ever made public, someone could read all the data in our database, delete our database or run up a huge cloud bill mining nonsense-coin. Therefore, it's best to avoid committing any sensitive data, like our JSON file, to our Git repository.</p> <h2 id="how-to-read-and-decrypt-a-file-before-initializing-the-firebase-sdk"><a href="#how-to-read-and-decrypt-a-file-before-initializing-the-firebase-sdk" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>How to Read and Decrypt a File before Initializing the Firebase SDK</h2> <p>Instead of storing the JSON file directly or as an environment variable, we can encrypt it and then decrypt it when we need to initialize the Firebase SDK. We can use the example code here: <a href="https://github.com/cyclic-software/example-secure-file" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://github.com/cyclic-software/example-secure-file</a></p> <h3 id="encrypt-your-file"><a href="#encrypt-your-file" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Encrypt your file</h3> <p>Follow the instructions in the repo, basically:</p> <ol> <li>clone</li> <li>add <code>SECRET_PASSPHRASE=<some long and secret passphrase></code> to <code>.env</code></li> <li>run <code>npm run encrypt serviceAccount.json</code></li> <li>copy the <code>serviceAccount.json.secure</code> file into your project</li> <li>copy the <code>secure-file.js</code> file into your project</li> <li>add <code>SECRET_PASSPHRASE=<some long and secret passphrase></code> to your project's environment variables</li> </ol> <h3 id="decrypt-on-init"><a href="#decrypt-on-init" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Decrypt on init</h3> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="line-numbers language-js"><code><span class="token keyword">const</span> admin <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token function">require</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token string">'firebase-admin'</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token keyword">const</span> <span class="token punctuation">{</span> decryptToString <span class="token punctuation">}</span> <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token function">require</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token string">'./secure-file.js'</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token comment">// replace with your location</span>
<span class="token keyword">const</span> secureFileName <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token string">'./serviceAccount.json.secure'</span> <span class="token comment">// replace with your filename</span> <span class="token keyword">const</span> jsonStr <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token keyword control-flow">await</span> <span class="token function">decryptToString</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>secureFileName<span class="token punctuation">)</span> <span class="token keyword">const</span> serviceAccount <span class="token operator">=</span> <span class="token known-class-name class-name">JSON</span><span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token method function property-access">parse</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>jsonStr<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span>
admin<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token method function property-access">initializeApp</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span><span class="token punctuation">{</span> <span class="token literal-property property">credential</span><span class="token operator">:</span> admin<span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token property-access">credential</span><span class="token punctuation">.</span><span class="token method function property-access">cert</span><span class="token punctuation">(</span>serviceAccount<span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">,</span> <span class="token punctuation">}</span><span class="token punctuation">)</span><span class="token punctuation">;</span> </code></pre></div> <h2 id="what-is-it-doing"><a href="#what-is-it-doing" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>What is it doing?</h2> <p>The <code>secure-file.js</code> code is using <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois/Counter_Mode" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">AES256 GCM</a> to symmetrically encrypt the input file. It also randomly generates an initialization vector (<code>iv</code>). It stores the <code>iv</code>, encrypted data and a signature of both, <code>auth_tag</code> to prevent against tampering. All three of these are stored in the <code>.secure</code> output file.</p> <p>Sample format:</p> <div class="nuxt-content-highlight"><pre class="line-numbers language-text"><code>{ "iv": "32-char-long-hex-string", "auth_tag": "32-char-long-hex-string", "data": "base64-encoded-encrypted-binary-data" } </code></pre></div> <h1 id="tldr"><a href="#tldr" aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>tldr</h1> <ol> <li>Don't store account secrets in git unless you want to let everyone crypto mine on your server.</li> <li>If you hit size limits on environment variables, consider using an encrypted secure file.</li> <li>Have a good time. Coding is fun.</li> </ol></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2 hover:no-underline hover:scale-105 transition w-full md:w-max"> Deploy on Cyclic 🚀 </a></div></section> <footer class="border-t border-white/20 py-16 px-6 sm:px-0 bg-black/20 backdrop-blur"><div border-b-white/10 pb-6"><h1 class="text-6xl font-black">How to Get Your First Developer Job</h1> <div class="flex items-center justify-between"><div class="flex items-center gap-3"><div class="flex flex-col border-r border-r-white/20 pr-3 text-gray-400"><span class="font-black text-2xl">22</span> <span class="uppercase text-xs font-medium tracking-widest"> Jul 2022 </span></div> <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-400">By Kam Lasater</span></div> <div class="text-xs px-2 py-1 border border-white/20 rounded-full capitalize text-gray-300"> Engineering </div></div></div> <div class="grid grid-cols-1"><div class="prose prose-xl prose-invert prose-a:text-sky-300 prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:border-sky-600 prose-h4:text-2xl prose-img:rounded-xl mx-auto w-full lg:w-max nuxt-content"><p>I've hired roughly 30 developers where the job would be their first professional position as a developer. I interviewed nearly 150 candidates. I reviewed resumes for about 300 candidates.</p> <p>None of this is certainly going to get you hired, the goal is to just improve your odds. Also, each hiring manager is different. Sometimes the person doing the screening and first line interview may not have ever coded. This advice is much geared to increasing your odds with a hiring manager who is technical.</p> <h2 id="github-timeline"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#github-timeline" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Github timeline</h2> <p>At the screening stage one powerful hack was to look at the applicat's Github timeline. All else being equal, I probably could have done ok just hiring the individuals with more activity in our target language.</p> <p>Looking at the GH timeline also was a good reality check against the career story that the candidate would tell.</p> <blockquote> <p>Oh I've really been getting into python and machine learning</p> </blockquote> <p>(checks github)</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/gh_timeline_inconsistent.png"></p> <p>no python repos, 3 commits in last 3 months. hmmm..</p> <p><strong>VS</strong></p> <blockquote> <p>I've been experimenting with a few front end frameworks hosted on different platforms to try to learn common coding and hosting patterns.</p> </blockquote> <p>(checks github)</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/gh_timeline_consistent.png"></p> <p>Four differnt front end framework repos, each a similar app, all hosted on free services. 3-5 commits a week for past few months.</p> <p>Notice how the second trajectory syncs to the history, whereas the first one doesn't. Given two candiates that seemed equally as strong I would lean towards the one that had a more consistent history. 3-5 dots / week for 6 months was better than a wall of comimts over the last 6 weeks.</p> <p><img alt="" src="/content/gh_timeline_wall.png"></p> <p><strong>tldr:</strong> As your math teacher said, show your work.</p> <h2 id="understanding-the-why"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#understanding-the-why" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Understanding the Why</h2> <p>As a manager I wanted to explain our goals as a company. Then explain our goals for a project. Then describe the feature we were looking to build. What button was needed on which page, or how to store what data only mattered in the context of the user/customer accomplishing their goal.</p> <p>During the interview process I wanted to see if the candidate was connected to the why of what they were doing and could explain how thier actions flowed from their own thinking connected to that why.</p> <p>Often times school projects have a constraint imposed to drive practice with a particular concept. This creates some areas of subtley in describing the why for those projects. Here is an example:</p> <p>Q: Why did you use Jupyter Notebooks and Pandas?</p> <p>A: I don't know. Its what we used for that class. The lab was to run word frequency analysis on books.</p> <p>vs</p> <p>A: The goal was to practice the NLP we were learning in class. I had been reading alot of Sci-Fi so thought it would be fun to do pro-noun usage comparisons between male and female authors. I couldn't find the data easily, but I found all the books for one author, so I compared the first half their career to second half.</p> <p>Even if</p> <p><strong>tldr:</strong> explain the goal not just the steps/techniques to achieve it.</p> <h2 id="story-telling"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#story-telling" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Story Telling</h2> <p>My experience of writing software is that it is a journey into the unknown. I need to study, learn and plan, but also respond to the unexpected. When interviewing I wanted to ensure that the candidates had the right skills and attitude to confront the unknown and find a way through.</p> <p>The best was when a story of debugging came up naturally. However sometimes I would try to prompt it with questions like:</p> <ul> <li>What problems did you encounter in that project? What did you learn?</li> <li>Tell me about a time you couldn't solve a technical problem, what did you do?</li> </ul> <p>I was looking to the candidate to be able to describe:</p> <ul> <li>what they attempted</li> <li>the why of what they were attempting</li> <li>what broke/failed</li> <li>how it failed</li> <li>their thinking about approach to solve</li> <li>what they tried to do to fix the issue that didn't work</li> <li>how they approached the failure</li> <li>the technical specifics of what they tried</li> <li>what the failure looked like</li> <li>their approach to find a solution</li> <li>how they fixed the issue</li> <li>the technical specifics of what they learned</li> </ul> <p><strong>tldr:</strong> writing software is solving problems you haven't solved, tell me a story of your hero's journey.</p> <h2 id="demonstration-of-team-ability--cooperation"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#demonstration-of-team-ability--cooperation" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Demonstration of Team Ability / Cooperation</h2> <p>Software is rarely built by one genius alone in a cave. Software and companies are a team sport. Rarely could I tell how good of a teammate someone would be. However, I certainly passed on candidates that didn't seem to have a collaborative orientation.</p> <p>Examples of failures:</p> <ul> <li>bad mouthing former teammates</li> <li>a pattern of interrupting me or talking over me during the interview</li> <li>using I to describe all the work done on a team project but then not being able to explain the details and only when pressed admitting that a team mate completed that part of the project</li> </ul> <p><strong>tldr:</strong> software is a team sport, show you can work well on a team</p> <h2 id="summary"><a aria-hidden="true" href="#summary" tabindex="-1"><span class="icon icon-link"></span></a>Summary</h2> <p>None of this will get you a job for sure. Hopefully this will help you improve your chances of getting hired. If you are just starting out on a career change or planning for a professional coding job, you can do it.</p> <ul> <li>Consistency beats intensity</li> <li>Be able to explain your thinking</li> <li>Software is a team sport</li> </ul></div></div></div> <section id="subscribe-form" class="common-section border !border-neutral-700 rounded-2xl w-full lg:w-[80%] px-7 py-10 bg-neutral-800/20"><div class="flex flex-col items-center text-center"><h2 class="font-bold text-4xl mb-4">Subscribe to posts</h2> <p>Enter your email If you would like to get an email the next time we post.<br>We post about ~1-2x per month, and up to once a month about company news.<br></p></div> <div class="mt-4"><div id="embedded-form"></div></div></section> <div class="relative w-full bg-neutral-800/20 border !border-neutral-700 rounded-xl flex flex-col items-center gap-5 text-center p-8"><h2 class="text-4xl font-bold">Launch a hello world</h2> <p class="w-full md:w-[50%] text-neutral-300"> Fork and deploy a hello world project onto Cyclic faster than it has taken to read this page. Experience the power. </p> <a href="https://app.cyclic.sh/api/login" target="_blank" class="bg-primary text-white capitalize flex items-center justify-center rounded-xl px-4 py-3 gap-2
